claim: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterial pathogen with a unique developmental cycle.
source: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterial pathogen with a unique developmental cycle.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the nature of C. trachomatis.

claim: Chlamydia trachomatis differentiates between two functional and morphological forms: the elementary body (EB) and the reticulate body (RB).
source: It differentiates between two functional and morphological forms: the elementary body (EB) and the reticulate body (RB).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the developmental forms.

claim: The signals that trigger differentiation from one form to the other are unknown.
source: The signals that trigger differentiation from one form to the other are unknown.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract indicating a knowledge gap.

claim: EBs and RBs have distinctive characteristics that distinguish them, including their size, infectivity, proteome, and transcriptome.
source: EBs and RBs have distinctive characteristics that distinguish them, including their size, infectivity, proteome, and transcriptome.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing differences between forms.

claim: EBs and RBs differ in their overall redox status as EBs are oxidized and RBs are reduced.
source: Intriguingly, they also differ in their overall redox status as EBs are oxidized and RBs are reduced.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing redox differences between forms.

claim: Alterations in redox may serve as a trigger for secondary differentiation.
source: We hypothesize that alterations in redox may serve as a trigger for secondary differentiation.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis stated in the abstract.

claim: AhpC is a well-known member of the peroxiredoxins family.
source: To test this, we examined the function of the primary antioxidant enzyme alkyl hydroperoxide reductase subunit C (AhpC), a well-known member of the peroxiredoxins family, in chlamydial growth and development.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing AhpC.

claim: During ahpC knockdown, ROS levels were elevated.
source: During ahpC knockdown, ROS levels were elevated, and the bacteria were sensitive to a broad set of peroxide stresses.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing experimental results.

claim: During ahpC knockdown, the bacteria were sensitive to a broad set of peroxide stresses.
source: During ahpC knockdown, ROS levels were elevated, and the bacteria were sensitive to a broad set of peroxide stresses.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing experimental results.

claim: During ahpC knockdown, increased expression of EB-associated genes was observed at an earlier time in the developmental cycle.
source: Interestingly, we observed increased expression of EB-associated genes and concurrent higher production of EBs at an earlier time in the developmental cycle, indicating earlier secondary differentiation occurs under elevated oxidation conditions.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing experimental results.

claim: During ahpC knockdown, higher production of EBs occurred at an earlier time in the developmental cycle.
source: Interestingly, we observed increased expression of EB-associated genes and concurrent higher production of EBs at an earlier time in the developmental cycle, indicating earlier secondary differentiation occurs under elevated oxidation conditions.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing experimental results.

claim: Earlier secondary differentiation occurs under elevated oxidation conditions.
source: Interestingly, we observed increased expression of EB-associated genes and concurrent higher production of EBs at an earlier time in the developmental cycle, indicating earlier secondary differentiation occurs under elevated oxidation conditions.
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of experimental results stated in the abstract.

claim: Overexpression of AhpC created a resistant phenotype against oxidizing agents.
source: In contrast, overexpression of AhpC created a resistant phenotype against oxidizing agents and delayed secondary differentiation.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing experimental results.

claim: Overexpression of AhpC delayed secondary differentiation.
source: In contrast, overexpression of AhpC created a resistant phenotype against oxidizing agents and delayed secondary differentiation.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing experimental results.

claim: Redox potential is a critical factor in developmental cycle progression.
source: Together, these results indicate that redox potential is a critical factor in developmental cycle progression.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion stated in the abstract based on experimental results.

claim: This study provides a mechanism of chlamydial secondary differentiation dependent on redox status.
source: For the first time, our study provides a mechanism of chlamydial secondary differentiation dependent on redox status.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the study's contribution.

claim: The process of metabolizing substrates in the presence of oxygen can generate reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are toxic at high enough concentrations.
source: Specifically, the process of metabolizing substrates in the presence of oxygen can generate reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are toxic at high enough concentrations.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing general biological knowledge.

claim: Systems have evolved from bacteria to humans to mitigate the accumulation of ROS.
source: Thus, from bacteria to humans, systems have evolved to mitigate the accumulation of ROS.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing general biological knowledge.

claim: Host immune defense mechanisms have evolved to leverage ROS production as a means of limiting pathogen growth and survival.
source: At the same time, host immune defense mechanisms have evolved to leverage ROS production as a means of limiting pathogen growth and survival.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing general biological knowledge.

claim: Pathogens have co-evolved to resist ROS-mediated defense mechanisms.
source: Not surprisingly, pathogens have co-evolved to resist these defense mechanisms.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing general biological knowledge.

claim: Many pathogens possess a variety of antioxidant enzymes, such as catalases, glutathione peroxidases, and peroxiredoxins.
source: For example, many pathogens possess a variety of antioxidant enzymes, such as catalases, glutathione peroxidases, and peroxiredoxins, that help them both subvert ROS-mediated immune system assaults and mitigate metabolic ROS byproducts (Staerck et al., 2017; Wan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular bacterium that has significantly reduced its genome size and content in adapting to obligate host dependence.
source: Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular bacterium that has significantly reduced its genome size and content in adapting to obligate host dependence.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing Chlamydia characteristics.

claim: Chlamydia trachomatis is the leading cause of bacterial sexually transmitted diseases.
source: Chlamydia trachomatis, the leading cause of bacterial sexually transmitted diseases and preventable infectious blindness, lacks homologs to catalases or glutathione peroxidases but does possess a homolog of AhpC.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing C. trachomatis.

claim: Chlamydia trachomatis is the leading cause of preventable infectious blindness.
source: Chlamydia trachomatis, the leading cause of bacterial sexually transmitted diseases and preventable infectious blindness, lacks homologs to catalases or glutathione peroxidases but does possess a homolog of AhpC.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing C. trachomatis.

claim: Chlamydia trachomatis lacks homologs to catalases or glutathione peroxidases.
source: Chlamydia trachomatis, the leading cause of bacterial sexually transmitted diseases and preventable infectious blindness, lacks homologs to catalases or glutathione peroxidases but does possess a homolog of AhpC.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing C. trachomatis genome.

claim: Chlamydia trachomatis possesses a homolog of AhpC.
source: Chlamydia trachomatis, the leading cause of bacterial sexually transmitted diseases and preventable infectious blindness, lacks homologs to catalases or glutathione peroxidases but does possess a homolog of AhpC.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing C. trachomatis genome.

claim: AhpC is a 2-cys peroxiredoxin that is widely conserved in prokaryotes.
source: AhpC is a 2-cys peroxiredoxin that is widely conserved in prokaryotes (de Oliveira et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: Peroxiredoxins scavenge hydrogen peroxide, peroxynitrite, and organic hydroperoxides.
source: Peroxiredoxins scavenge hydrogen peroxide, peroxynitrite, and organic hydroperoxides (Parsonage et al., 2008; Poole and Ellis, 1996; Seaver and Imlay, 2001) and act as the primary scavenger in pathogens that lack both catalase and glutathione peroxidases (Mastronicola et al., 2014; Richard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: Peroxiredoxins act as the primary scavenger in pathogens that lack both catalase and glutathione peroxidases.
source: Peroxiredoxins scavenge hydrogen peroxide, peroxynitrite, and organic hydroperoxides (Parsonage et al., 2008; Poole and Ellis, 1996; Seaver and Imlay, 2001) and act as the primary scavenger in pathogens that lack both catalase and glutathione peroxidases (Mastronicola et al., 2014; Richard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: AhpC has a significant role in ROS and RNI scavenging, virulence, and persistence in several bacterial systems.
source: Several studies from other bacterial systems have shown that AhpC has a significant role in ROS and RNI scavenging, virulence, and persistence (Cosgrove et al., 2007; Kimura et al., 2012; Oh and Jeon, 2014), and deletion of AhpC results in elevated levels of ROS within the bacterium (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: Deletion of AhpC results in elevated levels of ROS within the bacterium.
source: Several studies from other bacterial systems have shown that AhpC has a significant role in ROS and RNI scavenging, virulence, and persistence (Cosgrove et al., 2007; Kimura et al., 2012; Oh and Jeon, 2014), and deletion of AhpC results in elevated levels of ROS within the bacterium (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: Chlamydia is dependent on its host for most of its energy requirements.
source: Though Chlamydia is dependent on its host for most of its energy requirements, it has some metabolic activities, such as a partial TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation (Gérard et al., 2002; Iliffe-Lee and McClarty, 1999), which can be a possible source of intracellular ROS to which the bacteria must adapt.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: Chlamydia has some metabolic activities, such as a partial TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Though Chlamydia is dependent on its host for most of its energy requirements, it has some metabolic activities, such as a partial TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation (Gérard et al., 2002; Iliffe-Lee and McClarty, 1999), which can be a possible source of intracellular ROS to which the bacteria must adapt.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: Chlamydia's partial TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation can be a possible source of intracellular ROS.
source: Though Chlamydia is dependent on its host for most of its energy requirements, it has some metabolic activities, such as a partial TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation (Gérard et al., 2002; Iliffe-Lee and McClarty, 1999), which can be a possible source of intracellular ROS to which the bacteria must adapt.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: There is a paucity of knowledge on how C. trachomatis modulates oxidative stress.
source: There is a paucity of knowledge on how C. trachomatis modulates oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction indicating a knowledge gap.

claim: Infection of C. trachomatis induced the transient production of ROS by the host cell at a moderate level for the initial few hours of infection only.
source: However, some studies explored the effects of redox changes on chlamydial growth. Boncompain et al. reported that infection of C. trachomatis induced the transient production of ROS by the host cell at a moderate level for the initial few hours of infection only (Boncompain et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: Chlamydia requires host-derived ROS for its growth.
source: Another study also found a similar observation about ROS during infection, reporting that Chlamydia requires host-derived ROS for its growth (Abdul-Sater et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: The key mechanisms Chlamydia employs to manage ROS-mediated stress have not been characterized.
source: However, the key mechanisms Chlamydia employs to manage ROS-mediated stress have not been characterized.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction indicating a knowledge gap.

claim: Chlamydia undergoes a complex developmental cycle that comprises two distinct morphological forms, the EB and the RB.
source: Chlamydia undergoes a complex developmental cycle that comprises two distinct morphological forms, the EB and the RB (Abdelrahman and Belland, 2005).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: The EB is the smaller (~0.3 µm), infectious, and nondividing form capable of infecting susceptible host cells.
source: The EB is the smaller (~0.3 µm), infectious, and nondividing form capable of infecting susceptible host cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing EB characteristics.

claim: Once internalized into a host-derived vacuole termed an inclusion, the EB differentiates into the non-infectious, larger (~1 µm), and replicating RB.
source: Once internalized into a host-derived vacuole termed an inclusion, the EB differentiates into the non-infectious, larger (~1 µm), and replicating RB - this process is known as primary differentiation and represents the early phase of the developmental cycle (Clifton et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: The process of EB differentiating into RB is known as primary differentiation and represents the early phase of the developmental cycle.
source: Once internalized into a host-derived vacuole termed an inclusion, the EB differentiates into the non-infectious, larger (~1 µm), and replicating RB - this process is known as primary differentiation and represents the early phase of the developmental cycle (Clifton et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: RBs replicate within the inclusion in the midcycle phase using an asymmetric, MreB-dependent polarized division process.
source: RBs replicate within the inclusion in the midcycle phase using an asymmetric, MreB-dependent polarized division process (Abdelrahman et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2020; Ouellette et al., 2022; Ouellette et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: In the late phase of the developmental cycle, RBs asynchronously condense into EBs, and this process is termed secondary differentiation.
source: In the late phase of the developmental cycle, RBs asynchronously condense into EBs, and this process is termed secondary differentiation.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction describing secondary differentiation.

claim: How Chlamydia mechanistically differentiates between functional forms remains unclear.
source: Despite these well-defined differences between chlamydial morphological forms, how Chlamydia mechanistically differentiates between functional forms remains unclear.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction indicating a knowledge gap.

claim: RBs are reduced whereas EBs are oxidized.
source: Intriguingly, a recent study evaluated the redox potential of Chlamydia and demonstrated that RBs are reduced whereas EBs are oxidized (Wang et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: There are differences in the crosslinking of outer membrane proteins and type III secretion-related proteins in chlamydial developmental forms.
source: This is consistent with earlier studies that revealed differences in the crosslinking of outer membrane proteins and type III secretion-related proteins in chlamydial developmental forms (Betts-Hampikian and Fields, 2011; Caldwell et al., 1981; Everett and Hatch, 1995; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction with citation support.

claim: During the developmental cycle, the redox potential of Chlamydia is changing.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that, during the developmental cycle, the redox potential of Chlamydia is changing.
evidence: This is a direct inference stated in the introduction based on cited studies.

claim: Whether redox changes in Chlamydia directly affect developmental cycle progression is not characterized.
source: However, whether redox changes in Chlamydia directly affect developmental cycle progression is not characterized.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the introduction indicating a knowledge gap.

claim: Overexpression of ahpC increased the overall inclusion area at 14 and 24 hpi.
source: IFA imaging revealed that there was no observable impact on the morphology of the EV control strain under the conditions tested. In contrast, we did note that overexpression of ahpC increased the overall inclusion area (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to Figure 2B and C.

claim: Overexpression of ahpC resulted in a significant increase in gDNA levels at 24 hpi.
source: We next quantified the total number of bacteria (i.e., both RBs and EBs) by measuring genomic DNA and observed a significant increase in gDNA levels at 24 hpi in response to increased ahpC expression (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Recoverable inclusion forming units (IFUs) were significantly lower when overexpressing ahpC at 24 hpi.
source: Although inclusions were larger in area and contained more total bacteria as assessed by gDNA levels when overexpressing ahpC, recoverable inclusion forming units (IFUs: a measure of infectious EBs) were significantly lower under these conditions at 24 hpi (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: By 48 hpi, the difference in IFUs between induced and uninduced ahpC OE conditions was not statistically significant.
source: However, by 48 hpi, the difference between the induced and uninduced conditions, although still reduced, was not statistically significant.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results describing IFU data.

claim: AhpC overexpression skews the ratio of RBs to EBs, with a higher relative number of RBs and lower EBs at 24 hpi.
source: To test this, we calculated the ratio of IFUs to gDNA at 24 hpi, which revealed that the relative number of RBs is higher (and EBs lower) as a result of overexpression of ahpC (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: Overexpressing ahpC delays production of infectious EBs.
source: Overall, these data support the hypothesis that overexpressing ahpC delays production of infectious EBs.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion stated in the results based on experimental data.

claim: Both uninfected and EV-infected HeLa cells tolerated up to 1 mM oxidizing agents for 30 min, retaining more than 90% viability.
source: Both uninfected and EV-infected HeLa cells tolerated up to 1 mM oxidizing agents for 30 min, retaining more than 90% viability (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: 62.5 µM concentration of all three inorganic and organic peroxides had no appreciable effect on IFUs of WT Ctr L2.
source: 62.5 µM concentration of all three inorganic and organic peroxides had no appreciable effect on IFUs, and inclusion size and morphology also remained unaffected at this sublethal concentration.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results describing experimental observations.

claim: The concentrations of inorganic and organic peroxides that resulted in a decrease in IFUs to ~50% of the untreated culture were 500 µM (H2O2) and 250 µM (CHP and TBHP).
source: The concentrations of inorganic and organic peroxides that resulted in a decrease in IFUs to ~50% of the untreated culture were 500 µM (H2O2) and 250 µM (CHP and TBHP), respectively, with a concurrent decrease in inclusion size.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results describing experimental observations.

claim: 1 mM H2O2, CHP, and TBHP caused >90% reduction in IFUs and small inclusions.
source: 1 mM H2O2, CHP, and TBHP caused >90% reduction in IFUs and small inclusions.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results describing experimental observations.

claim: PN at 1 mM concentration was less effective than other oxidizing agents and showed only a ~30% decline in IFUs compared to the untreated culture.
source: PN at 1 mM concentration was less effective than other oxidizing agents and showed only a ~30% decline in IFUs compared to the untreated culture (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: The ahpC overexpression strain showed increased resistance to all oxidants tested as the mean IFUs and the size of inclusions were greater than that of the uninduced but treated control.
source: As shown in Figure 3A and B, and Supplement 3, the ahpC overexpression strain showed increased resistance to all oxidants tested as the mean IFUs and the size of inclusions were greater than that of the uninduced but treated control.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to figures.

claim: The resistant phenotype of ahpC overexpression was more evident at the higher concentrations of H2O2, CHP, and TBHP.
source: The resistant phenotype was more evident at the higher concentrations of H2O2, CHP, and TBHP.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results describing experimental observations.

claim: Overexpression of ahpC contributed to higher resistance against PN.
source: Overexpression of ahpC also contributed to higher resistance against PN.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results describing experimental observations.

claim: The empty vector control strain behaved as expected (i.e., like WT) in the presence of oxidizing agents.
source: Conversely, the empty vector control strain behaved as expected (i.e., like WT) in the presence of oxidizing agents, with similar results observed in the presence or absence of aTc (Figure 3C, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to figures.

claim: The chlamydial AhpC possesses antioxidant activity.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that the chlamydial AhpC possesses antioxidant activity, as expected, and that increased ahpC expression is protective for Chlamydia in the presence of increased oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion stated in the results based on experimental data.

claim: Increased ahpC expression is protective for Chlamydia in the presence of increased oxidative stress.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that the chlamydial AhpC possesses antioxidant activity, as expected, and that increased ahpC expression is protective for Chlamydia in the presence of increased oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion stated in the results based on experimental data.

claim: ahpC knockdown resulted in approximately 90% reduction of ahpC transcripts compared to the uninduced control.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of the ahpC KD revealed approximately 90% reduction of ahpC transcripts compared to the uninduced control, thus confirming the knockdown of ahpC (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: IFA of ahpC knockdown strains revealed noticeably smaller inclusions after blocking expression of ahpC as compared to the uninduced sample or the NT conditions.
source: IFA of these strains revealed noticeably smaller inclusions after blocking expression of ahpC as compared to the uninduced sample or the NT conditions (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: During ahpC knockdown, higher gDNA levels were observed at 14 hpi compared to the uninduced control, followed by only a small increase from 14 to 24 hpi.
source: Surprisingly, even though inclusions were smaller during ahpC knockdown, we observed higher gDNA levels at 14 hpi compared to the uninduced control, followed by only a small increase from 14 to 24 hpi (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: The uninduced ahpC KD strain showed a logarithmic increase in gDNA levels from 14 to 24 hpi, similar to the NT strain.
source: In contrast, the uninduced strain showed a logarithmic increase in gDNA levels during this timeframe, similar to the NT strain (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: IFU analysis exhibited severely reduced progeny (>90%) during ahpC knockdown conditions compared to its respective uninduced control at both 24 and 48 hpi.
source: IFU analysis exhibited severely reduced progeny (>90%) during ahpC knockdown conditions compared to its respective uninduced control at both time points assessed (24 and 48 hpi) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: The NT strain showed less than a 50% reduction in IFUs after inducing dCas12 expression at 24 and 48 hpi.
source: In contrast, the NT strain showed less than a 50% reduction after inducing dCas12 expression at these timepoints consistent with prior observations that dCas12 expression slightly delays developmental cycle progression (Hatch and Ouellette, 2023; Reuter et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with citation support.

claim: The ratio of IFUs to gDNA at 24 hpi is significantly higher for the ahpC KD, suggesting a lower number of RBs in proportion to EBs.
source: The ratio of IFUs to gDNA at 24 hpi is significantly higher for the ahpC KD, suggesting a lower number of RBs in proportion to EBs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: Reducing ahpC levels and/or activity severely reduced chlamydial growth at 24 and 48 hpi.
source: Taken together, these analyses indicate that reducing ahpC levels and/or activity severely reduced chlamydial growth at 24 and 48 hpi.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion stated in the results based on experimental data.

claim: ahpC knockdown resulted in significantly higher ROS than the uninfected or infected but uninduced samples at both 24 hpi and 48 hpi time points.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, ahpC knockdown resulted in significantly higher ROS than the uninfected or infected but uninduced samples at both 24 hpi and 48 hpi time points.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Live-cell microscopy images revealed that ahpC KD resulted in higher ROS in comparison to the uninduced and uninfected cells.
source: We also performed live-cell microscopy for visualization of ROS generation in uninfected and ahpC KD-infected HeLa cells at 24 and 40 hpi. These microscopy images revealed that ahpC KD resulted in higher ROS in comparison to the uninduced and uninfected cells (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to figures.

claim: The ROS signal was associated with chlamydial inclusions and not the host cell.
source: Importantly, the signal was associated with chlamydial inclusions and not the host cell, thus indicating that the measurements from Figure 5A were from the bacteria.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results describing microscopy observations.

claim: AhpC knockdown results in increased ROS levels in C. trachomatis.
source: These results together indicate that AhpC knockdown results in increased ROS levels in C. trachomatis.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion stated in the results based on experimental data.

claim: Under conditions of ahpC knockdown, even sublethal concentrations (62.5 µM) of H2O2, CHP, or TBHP further reduced the inclusion size.
source: Under conditions of ahpC knockdown, even sublethal concentrations (62.5 µM) of H2O2, CHP, or TBHP further reduced the inclusion size, and the IFU data revealed a decrease from >90% to <30% in comparison to the untreated control (Figure 6A, B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to figures.

claim: Under conditions of ahpC knockdown, IFUs decreased from >90% to <30% in comparison to the untreated control when exposed to sublethal concentrations of oxidizing agents.
source: Under conditions of ahpC knockdown, even sublethal concentrations (62.5 µM) of H2O2, CHP, or TBHP further reduced the inclusion size, and the IFU data revealed a decrease from >90% to <30% in comparison to the untreated control (Figure 6A, B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to figures.

claim: Reduced expression of ahpC affected the survival of Chlamydia against peroxynitrite.
source: Reduced expression of ahpC also affected the survival of Chlamydia against peroxynitrite.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results describing experimental observations.

claim: There was no significant change in the NT control strain in the uninduced and induced samples in response to oxidizing agents as assessed by IFU and IFA.
source: Notably, there was no significant change in the NT control strain in the uninduced and induced samples in response to oxidizing agents as assessed by IFU and IFA (Figure 6C, D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to figures.

claim: The chlamydial AhpC is a critical antioxidant enzyme in these bacteria.
source: These data further support that the chlamydial AhpC is a critical antioxidant enzyme in these bacteria.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion stated in the results based on experimental data.

claim: Increased transcripts for ahpC were quantified under complementation conditions, indicating successful complementation of the knockdown effect.
source: After inducing dCas12-ahpC expression with aTc, the resultant strain was verified by RT-qPCR. Increased transcripts for ahpC were quantified under these conditions, indicating successful complementation of the knockdown effect (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: Complementation of ahpC knockdown revealed normal inclusion morphology, gDNA levels, and EB progeny production.
source: These assays revealed normal inclusion morphology, gDNA levels, and EB progeny production in the complemented strain, indicating successful complementation of the knockdown phenotype (Figure 7B, C and D).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to figures.

claim: A C-terminal 6xHis tagged AhpC was not capable of complementing the knockdown phenotype.
source: Of note, a C-terminal 6xHis tagged AhpC was not capable of complementing the knockdown phenotype (data not shown), indicating a requirement for a free C-terminus in the function of AhpC in Chlamydia.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results describing experimental observations.

claim: There is a requirement for a free C-terminus in the function of AhpC in Chlamydia.
source: Of note, a C-terminal 6xHis tagged AhpC was not capable of complementing the knockdown phenotype (data not shown), indicating a requirement for a free C-terminus in the function of AhpC in Chlamydia.
evidence: This is a direct inference stated in the results based on experimental observations.

claim: The C-terminal residues in AhpC play a crucial role in the structural stability and enzymatic activity of AhpC.
source: Previous studies in other bacteria have revealed that the C-terminal residues in AhpC play a crucial role in the structural stability and enzymatic activity of AhpC (Dip et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2020; Wan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with citation support.

claim: The complemented strain showed wild-type responses to sublethal concentrations of oxidizing agents.
source: Consistent with the growth parameters (Figure 7B–D), the complemented strain showed wild-type responses in these conditions (Figure 7E, F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to figures.

claim: The enhanced susceptibility of the ahpC knockdown strain to oxidizing agents was due to the reduced levels of ahpC and not an indirect effect of knockdown.
source: These data indicate that the enhanced susceptibility of the ahpC knockdown strain to oxidizing agents was due to the reduced levels of ahpC and not an indirect effect of knockdown.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion stated in the results based on experimental data.

claim: 10 mM DMTU and 100 µM α-tocopherol had no adverse effects on uninfected or EV-infected HeLa cells.
source: This assay revealed that 10 mM DMTU and 100 µM α-tocopherol had no adverse effects on uninfected or EV-infected HeLa cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results describing experimental observations.

claim: ROS scavengers restored IFUs from ~50% to ~100% in WT Ctr L2 treated with 500 µM H2O2, and inclusion size was also recovered.
source: In the case of peroxide (500 µM H2O2) treated samples, scavengers restored IFUs from ~50% to ~100%, and inclusion size was also recovered (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the results with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: Both ROS scavengers had a positive impact on restoring the growth of the ahpC knockdown strain; inclusions were larger, and IFUs were increased from <10% to >90% in the presence of scavengers in the induced samples.
